items.title: The Handwritten Final Draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' Speech Was Considered Lost. It Turned Out to Be Sitting in a Desk Drawer for Decades
items.desc: Across seven yellow notepad pages, King is seen wrestling with word choice and revising his remarks the night before the March on Washington. The manuscript will head to auction in January and is expected to pull in more than $10 million
items.text:
It was late on August 27, 1963, and Martin Luther King Jr. was huddled with a group of his closest advisors in the lobby of the Willard Hotel in Washington, D.C.
They were drafting King’s closing remarks for the March on Washington , officially the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, which was set to start in just 12 hours. The group went back and forth on the message: Should it be ideological or Biblical? Directed towards the students marching or the nation at large?
As the night wore on, King eventually bowed out. “Okay brothers,” Clarence B. Jones , an activist and speechwriter for King, recalled him saying. “Thank you so much everybody for your suggestions and input … I am now going upstairs to my room to counsel with my Lord.”
Alone in his suite, King stayed up until 4 a.m., writing and revising his remarks on a yellow notepad, scratching out swaths of text in blue ink. He then sent these marked-up pages to be typed, forming the basis of his canonical “I Have a Dream” speech , delivered to more than 250,000 demonstrators gathered by the Lincoln Memorial .
Scholars have long assumed that the original, handwritten final draft had been discarded amid the day’s chaos. But six decades later, the manuscript has resurfaced from a drawer of one of King’s former aides. The seven yellow pages are set to be auctioned at Christie’s in January, where the draft is expected to sell for more than $10 million.
“When I first saw these pages and realized what they were, I was astounded,” Christie’s manuscripts specialist Peter Klarnet says in a statement . “This is a treasure of American history … Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr. King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time.”
Civil rights leader and philanthropist Xernona Clayton found the pages in the late 1990s. They were tucked in an envelope labeled “speech,” nestled among other papers in a desk drawer belonging to her late husband, Edward , one of King’s aides and speechwriters.
Clayton knew it was an important document related to the “I Have a Dream” speech but not that it was the final manuscript. She tucked it back in the desk drawer, not wanting to disrespect King’s memory by selling or displaying his memorabilia.
But in recent years, she changed her mind. “Now that I’m older, I’m wiser,” Clayton, now 96, tells the New York Times ’ Jennifer Schuessler. “It just seems like something that important ought to be shared.”

items.text:
At first glance, the soft, pastel-colored illustrations of San Marino-based artist Nicoletta Ceccoli appear sweet and innocent. However, beneath their cute appearance, her illustrations explore darker psychological themes. Her new solo exhibition, titled Under My Spell , at Corey Helford Gallery in LA explores fear, desire, emotional dependency, identity, and control.
For the last two decades, Ceccoli has been creating surreal, fairytale-like worlds that are both enchanting and unsettling. Her childlike figures inhabit fantastical landscapes filled with flowers, toys, sweets and mysterious creatures, but something darker often lurks beneath the surface. In one image, a candy dispenser is depicted as a trap, and in another, a childhood birthday party seems more like a strange nightmare.
Ceccoli’s work is a reminder of how desire can often lead to dependency, or how longing for human connection can sometimes erode your self-love and ability to set boundaries. She explains that her work visualizes “a story of a place where desires and fears, light and shadow coexist.” She adds, “Wonder is always touched by unease, and sweetness conceals something darker within a fragile balance.”
Under My Spell is currently showing in Gallery 3 of Corey Helford Gallery until December 5, 2026. You can also keep up to date with the artist’s work by following Nicoletta Ceccoli on Instagram .

items.text:
“He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail.” That’s how one rescuer in Kentucky described the moment he spotted 6-year-old Roman Heilman, a boy with autism missing for 3 days.
Jacob Mullins, a member of a local horse trailriding group, told the Lexington Herald Leader that he was only about a half-mile from Heilman’s home when he suddenly climbed out of a bush followed by a small dog, and and sang “Old McDonald.”
Heilman then grabbed onto the leg of the lead rescuer and didn’t want to let go.
He had been reported missing in the late afternoon on Sunday, November 1st, and the volunteers had been out since first light on Tuesday, looking around the wooded and mountainous area for hours, covering some 14 miles.
1 of 10 members of a horse trailriding group who live either side of the Kentucky-West Virginia state line, Jacob Mullins told the Lexington Herald Leader about the moment that the hunters became the hunted.
“We found him probably about a mile and a half from his house. He came out of the bushes saying ‘E-I-E-I-O horsey.’ He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail,” Mullins remembered.
“He was naked, and he was scratched, and he had a little dog with him. He ate a banana and drank some water and then we brought him off the hill.”
Roman is autistic, and when it was reported to police that he had wandered away from his house into the woods, “hundreds” volunteered to aid in the search. This included other teams on horseback, drones, but also motor vehicles, which Mullins thought perhaps had scared the boy from being found earlier.
Rescue authorities had received information on Sunday that the child had removed his clothing at some point, making the situation even more concerning. Indeed, he would have spent two frigid nights in the woods.
Travis Hughes, Director of Lawrence County Emergency Management, put out a heartfelt statement following the rescue on Facebook, in which he said he had “never been more proud” of the community.

“I have always said that when something happens here in Lawrence County, our people come together. But what I witnessed during this search was truly something special.”

items.title: A glimmer of good news for Britain's sleepy dormouse
items.desc: New figures suggest hazel dormice may be recovering after decades of decline, with warmer summers boosting survival.
items.text:
Dormice have become much rarer in the UK as woodlands and hedgerows are lost
Dormouse numbers may be recovering in England and Wales after years of decline, offering a rare piece of good news for one of our best-loved mammals.
The animal has disappeared from much of the countryside with conservationists warning of a long-term collapse in its population.
However, new data suggests dormouse numbers increased between 2020-2025, a period that coincided with warmer springs and summers.
Scientists believe these conditions may help dormice survive, by boosting food supplies and reducing the time they spend asleep.
That gives the animals more opportunity to breed and build up fat reserves ahead of winter.
Even during spring and summer, when it's cold and wet, dormice can go into short periods of deep sleep
But conservationists caution that many questions remain unanswered, and say protecting the woodlands and hedgerows where dormice live remains essential to their long-term survival.
The only native species of dormice in the UK is the hazel dormouse. Once widespread across the country, they are now largely confined to southern England and parts of Wales. They have become much rarer as large areas of woodland are lost and so far native populations have disappeared from around 20 English counties.
The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme, led by the conservation charity People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES), has been monitoring sites in England and Wales since 1998.
It found that since 2000, dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60%, equivalent to an average annual decline of 3.5%.
More recently, however, there are signs that trend may be reversing. The data suggests the population increased by almost 10% between 2020 and 2025, although researchers stress there is considerable uncertainty around that estimate.
The apparent improvement coincides with a period of warmer, drier-than-average springs and summers.
Report co-author Ian White of PTES described the "upturn" as "welcome good news" which gives grounds for "cautious optimism".
But he added: "We mustn't lose sight of the bigger picture: populations remain almost 60% lower than they were in 2000."
The hazel dormouse spends most of its time in trees, coming out at night to eat flowers, insects, berries and nuts

items.title: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
items.desc: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
items.text:
Swans and ducks have enjoyed the wetland reserve at Slimbridge for 80 years
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.
Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).
Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.
Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."
Sir Peter Scott feeds migrating swans and geese at Slimbridge in 1947, with Desmond Hawkins, BBC features producer from Bristol
WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.
Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change.
So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change?
The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes.
Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl.
He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them.
Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl.
Sir Peter Scott with the first nine Nēnē geese he hand-reared at Slimbridge in 1952
"He really was a pioneer in conservation," said Chris Moore, a historian of Slimbridge and author of Peter Scott and the Birth of Modern Conservation.
As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature.
He led the fight to stop commercial whaling, presented some of the BBC's first natural history programmes called live from Slimbridge, and helped set up WWF, the World Wildlife Fund.

61 years ago today, the ironically-named Murder Act of 1965 is given Royal Assent, formally abolishing the death penalty in the United Kingdom for almost all crimes. Introduced by MP for Liverpool Sydney Silverman, it replaced hanging with mandatory sentences of life-imprisonment in all but 4 cases. The outstanding exceptions related to military-intelligence crimes, such as piracy with the intent to cause grievous injury, high treason, and espionage. READ more… (1965)
No executions have occurred in the United Kingdom since the Murder Act of 1965. The last were on August 13th, 1964, when Peter Allen and Gwynne Evans were hanged for murdering John Alan West during a theft four months earlier.
During the Troubles Westminster passed the Northern Ireland Constitution Act 1973, abolishing Stormont, and the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1973, abolishing the death penalty for murder there. The death penalty was not fully abolished in the United Kingdom until 1998 by the Human Rights Act 1998 and the Crime and Disorder Act 1998.
735 years ago today, the Republic of Venice passed a law confining the city’s growing glassmaking industry to the island of Murano , giving birth to the tradition of Murano glass, one of the city’s most iconic characteristics. In the following century, exports began, and the island became famous, initially for glass beads and mirrors. Aventurine glass was invented on the island, and for a while Murano was the main producer of glass in Europe. Today, it’s a craft that is entering the fine art world.
From practical items like cups, bowls, lamps, and chandeliers, Murano artisans gradually began turning from applied art to fine art, with chandeliers becoming works of sculpture, and works of sculpture becoming masterpieces.
While the glass itself is delicate and dainty, a Murano glass artisan must be physically durable and resilient. Once he or she starts a piece, they cannot stop until it’s finished even if that means 16 hours of work. Neither the artisan, nor the glass can be allowed to cool down too much from the incredible heat of the furnaces, otherwise, the molten glass won’t be shapable anymore.
Murano glass artwork is now a more sensible business model for these artisans, as the high cost they merit is more flexible and can absorb higher energy prices in Europe as natural gas is needed to heat the furnaces.

items.text:
A viral moment from a doorbell camera that reached millions of people has now raised more than $76,000 to support a woman who spends her days caring for others.
When Suzanna Metcalf arrived at Pastor Neal Seiwert’s home in Castle Rock, Colorado last year, she apologized as she had mixed up their pizza order, and would have to return with the correct order. She blamed “getting old,” but the struggle on her face was clear.
Metcalf works delivery shifts while serving as the full-time caregiver for her 82-year-old mother, managing daily care, medical needs and household expenses.
Instead of frustration, Seiwert, his wife Hailee, and their three young daughters stepped outside, placed their hands on her shoulders, and prayed for her. The short clip, captured by a doorbell camera, showed Metcalf visibly moved by the unexpected kindness after a long day of work.
The video, posted by Seiwert, quickly went viral, with hundreds of commenters, who almost all had the same question: How can we help?
The Seiwerts found Metcalf, and with her permission, started a GoFundMe, which describes Suzanna as a woman who has spent years putting others first.
What began as a modest effort quickly grew. More than 2,600 donors have contributed over the last year, raising over $76,000 — far exceeding the initial $10,000 goal— to give Suzanna some financial breathing room as she continues caring for her mom.
Seiwert told the New York Post he wanted Metcalf to feel both his family’s support and a broader sense of being valued. “So many people are commenting on how it brought them to tears. There are many people who simply just need love,” he said.
A viral moment doesn’t change the demands of caregiving and delivery work. But it has shown, in concrete form, that one small pause for kindness can open the door for real help.

Since its advent, photography has changed the way we experience and remember culture. Portrait photography, in particular, helps to catalog those who have an outsized impact on society. A forthcoming exhibition at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery looks back at portrait photography, what it can tell us about American history and culture, and how it helped shape the two. The show, titled Photographic Memory: Fifty Years of Collecting , features more than 120 works from the institution’s collection—including never-before-exhibited pieces.
Photographic Memory celebrates the 50th anniversary of the Portrait Gallery’s photographic repertoire. Photos now account for nearly half of the museum’s total holdings, but that wasn’t always the case. Photography didn’t enter the museum’s collection until 1976—the year of the U.S. bicentennial—when it expanded its collecting mandate to include photography. This shift mattered; without it, the Portrait Gallery couldn’t feature people important in U.S. history who never sat for a painted portrait or posed for a sculpture.
Although the show covers 50 years of collecting, some photographs in the exhibition are much older. One notable work includes a 1846 daguerreotype (the first publicly available photo process) of Dolley Madison by John Plumbe Jr. In the show, it’s paired with a 1843 half-plate daguerreotype of President John Quincy Adams. This marks the first time that the earliest known photograph of a U.S. president and a first lady have been shown together.
Other pieces in Photographic Memory include iconic images and people beyond politicians. These works include Alexander Gardner’s original “cracked plate” portrait of Abraham Lincoln, images of athletes like Muhammad Ali, singers including Billie Holiday, and artists such as Georgia O’Keeffe and Isamu Noguchi . The exhibition also debuts a portrait of poet and author Amanda Gorman, photographed by Shawn Theodore, and a portrait of actor and activist Christopher Reeve by Herb Ritts. The exhibition also features influential photographers, including Alfred Stieglitz, Dorothea Lange , Ansel Adams , and Gordon Parks .

items.text:
Just a few weeks ago it was the driest place on Earth. Now it’s the most colorful.
Chile’s Atacama Desert has erupted into perhaps the greatest floral display ever recorded there, with some 200 species blooming—some in areas where flowers haven’t been seen since the before new millennium.
VIDEO: 🇨🇱 Chile's Atacama Desert fills with flowers in spring The phenomenon, known as the "flowering desert," occurs in certain years when rainfall and temperatures coincide, awakening the desert's dormant seeds #AFPVertical https://t.co/Cr4C3LaFa8
It means that seeds and tubers have lain dormant under the sand waiting for the lifegiving touch of water for decades—a remarkable adaptation. For the people who protect this desert ecosystem, it’s another reminder of the incredible resilience and diversity of life that makes this place worth protecting.
“This is a natural seed bank, a dormant archive that becomes a living one with the rains,” Moisés Grimberg, the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park in the Atacama, told NPR, whose images of the flowering have to be seen to be believed.
“But it’s a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months.”
This year’s Super El Niño weather event dumped record rainfall onto the landscape. Through July and August, flooding allowed water to permeate deep into the soil, touching seeds that normally escape seasonal rains.
The resulting “superbloom,” to use the California term, is easily the widest-reaching and most vivid in 30 years. It’s a record that might not stand for long though, as the world’s driest, non-polar desert is seeing more rainfall than usual.
NPR says the increased frequency of the seasonal rains are creating conditions for more varied animal life—albeit transiently—such as reptiles, insects, bats and other pollinators, and even larger animals like the iconic guanaco, a relative of the lama.

17 years ago today, Utah Jazz coach Jerry Sloan became the first in professional basketball history to win 1,000 games with a single team. Described as “one of the greatest and most respected coaches in NBA history,” he spent nearly his entire 23-year coaching career at Utah, managing the team through good times and bad, leading some spectacular talent such as Carlos Boozer and Karl Malone, and making the Western Conference playoffs 16 times in a row. “Winning’s fine,” Sloan said, after the match, “but that’s a short-lived thing. Losing sticks with you for a long time.”
The victory of 104 to 97 over Oklahoma City meant Sloan’s record was 1,000 to 596, an average of 50 wins a season, or a nearly bang on 60% win rate, an impressive feat considering the grind of the NBA. In fact, he was one of three coaches in NBA history at the time to win 50 or more games on 10 separate occasions.
Under him, the Jazz had only one losing season in the past 20 by 2009. His teams made the playoffs 18 times, and he took them to 16 straight winning seasons (1988-2004), the second-longest streak in league history.
Happy Birthday to Joni Mitchell who turns 82 today. The Canadian singer-songwriter and painter is one of the most influential female musicians of the late 20th century. Her many hit songs include ” Both Sides Now ,” “ Chelsea Morning ,” “ Big Yellow Taxi, ” “ A Case of You ,” “ River, ” “ California, ” and “ Free Man in Paris ”—all recorded before she was 32.
Her distinctive open-tuned guitar was prompted by her childhood bout with polio which afflicted her fingers. Joni said the improvised tuning freed her songwriting, and was “a tool to break free of standard approaches to harmony and structure”.
Five years ago she suffered a brain aneurysm and she also suffers from a rare disorder called Morgellons disease. In recent years she channeled her creativity into a book of drawings and writings, Morning Glory on the Vine: Early Songs and Drawings , and a biography about her life, Reckless Daughter , which was released in 2017. Birds share our everyday spaces, but we rarely take the time to really notice how they’ve adapted to living among us. NIDIUM by SPLACES.STUDIO is an ongoing series of nest-like, audio-reactive sculptures that invite us to pause and listen to birdsong .
The name NIDIUM comes from the Latin word for “nest.” The installation series comprises 20 unique public sculptures of varying sizes, measuring between 2.5 and 4 meters (8.2 to 13.1 feet) in diameter. Woven from cultivated willow, each larger-than-life nest is interlaced with warm strips of LED lighting and emits a continuous soundscape of birdsong recorded in Karelia, between northwestern Russia and Finland.
Each sculpture “listens” to the sounds around it, responding with its own unique soundscape based on human voices and movements. This creates a playful two-way conversation between people and nature, helping observers become more aware of the wildlife sharing their surroundings.
The series is a collaborative effort, brought to life by artist Andre Svibovitch , light engineer Nikita Boyak , floral artist Sabir Ahmedov , sound programmer Vsevolod Krassa, and neural network specialist Igor Prudnikov. Each sculpture is individually programmed and made with slightly different forms, allowing the giant nests to fit into a range of locations, from urban environments to exhibition spaces. So far, NIDIUM installations have appeared in skyscrapers and public spaces across St. Petersburg, as well as at Bolzano Art Week and various exhibitions throughout Europe and North America.

items.title: Even Replacing Some of Your Dietary Dairy With Plant-Based Alternatives Can Lead to Nutrient Deficiencies, Study Suggests
items.desc: More people are swapping animal products with vegan milks, yogurts and cheeses, so scientists wanted to investigate the potential public health effects. Their findings hint that consumers should look for items with extra nutrients added, called fortified foods
items.text:
Alternative dairy products are widely available in many countries. Grocery stores and cafes frequently offer “milks” made from soy, almond, oat, rice or other crops. That’s good news for people who don’t consume dairy, as well as for our planet, since the production of plant-based milk is more environmentally friendly than regular milk.
But relying on these plant-based alternatives—even partially—might carry health risks. In a study published in the September issue of the journal Lancet Planetary Health , researchers ran computer simulations based on United Kingdom nutrition data and found that swapping standard dairy for vegan versions can lead to deficiencies of four vital nutrients. However, that could be combated by mandating that nutrients be added to plant-based dairy alternatives, as well as bread, making them fortified foods .
Vegan milks, cheeses, yogurts, ice creams and more are becoming increasingly popular as people turn to them for health or sustainability reasons. However, they often lack certain nutrients found in dairy.
To explore the potential public health implications, researchers pulled data from the U.K.’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey involving more than 3,500 people between the ages of 1.5 and 100 years old. They put that information into a computer model to simulate how swapping out regular milk, yogurt and cheese with commercially available plant-based versions affected intake of four micronutrients: iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12.
The results weren’t great. Even replacing a modest amount of dairy caused a decline in intake of all analyzed micronutrients. Iodine took the biggest hit. Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make certain hormones, and it’s also crucial for brain development. The micronutrient is especially important for infants, adolescents and pregnant people.
The survey data revealed that 54 percent of girls ages 14 to 18 weren’t eating enough iodine. Replacing just 35 percent of dairy with plant-based alternatives would cause the deficiency to jump to 65 percent. Similarly, 32 percent of women ages 19 to 49 were iodine deficient at baseline, and it would rise to 42 percent after the same dairy swap.
If dairy intake was completely replaced, 80 percent of teenage girls and 72 percent of teenage boys would be iodine deficient, according to the computer simulations.

While most people are putting their feet up in retirement, 103-year-old World War II veteran Irvin Koch is still keeping busy at his popular basement bar in Pasadena, Maryland. He’s been running his humble, fully licensed establishment for 60 years, where generations of customers regularly gather for a drink.
Koch served in the Philippines with the Navy, and when the war ended, he was 22 years old. Years later, in 1963, he and his brother bought a house in Pasadena that came with an unexpected bar in the basement. Rather than getting rid of it, he decided to open his very own dive bar called Sunset Knoll Club, now known as Irv’s Basement Bar. Six decades later, the drinks continue to flow, the regulars keep coming, the old jukebox keeps playing, and the original decor has barely changed.
Irv’s Basement Bar is full of quirky details, but the dozens of bras dangling from the ceiling are perhaps the most unexpected feature. Apparently, the collection has grown over the years as female customers have donated their own, often leaving their names behind as well. Irv can even recall who started the tradition—a customer named Amy. Visitors will also find names and messages scribbled across the bar counter, walls, and tables, left by other patrons who’ve visited the bar over the years.
Despite being tucked away in his home, the bar is officially recognized as a commercial establishment. And although Koch insists he stays open purely for the cash, his stepson, Jason Cook, believes there’s more to it. “He loves interacting with people and socializing,” he reveals . “He also likes being the center of attention. That certainly seems to be what’s keeping him alive.”

items.text:
GNN Voices is a new series of first-person pieces from people worth listening to: practitioners, researchers, teachers, and neighbors sharing what they’ve learned and how they see things.
My dad’s name was Kiran. In Sanskrit, it means “a ray of light.”
I wrote my book, Making Sense of Purpose , in his memory. His name is in the subtitle.
My dad found a way to walk with people without carrying them; he found a way to guide them without giving them directions; he held space, he held hands, he held space for their wants, needs and expectations, and then he shined a light on what made them and mattered to them and what’s forward …
This week is Diwali, the festival of lights. This year, I want to make it a gift to everyone. A week to shine a light back on the year and move forward with purpose before we rush into the new one.
Wanting to avoid a doom scroll is hard. But giving people something to do instead maybe helps.
It happens more because of the environment we built than because of any flaw in us. We grab what fills us without considering whether it nourishes us.
A few minutes of reflection pays us back. Researchers at Harvard Business School found that new employees who spent the last 15 minutes of each training day writing and reflecting on what they’d learned performed 22.8% better on their final test.
Ten questions. Five days. One in the morning, one at night. A few minutes each. Write it down, or just reflect and take note. Either way counts.
We’re bad at knowing what will make us happy. We rarely get explicit about what made a good moment good. So we never ask people what made them happy; we ask what makes them smile as they reflect.
We are strengths to be harnessed. Not weaknesses to be fixed. And our values are who we are when the world is at its messiest. Kennon Sheldon and Andrew Elliot found that when our goals come from our values, we put in more sustained effort and are more likely to reach them.
Not every plateau needs to be broken. Self-forgiveness is the single most powerful action, wholly within your control, that allows you to empty your backpack. When we forgive ourselves, the likelihood going forward is that we’ll be faster to break free than if we carry the guilt forward. And big wins are made by small steps.
As David McRaney puts it, Anxiety = Fear + Uncertainty. Sorting what we can control, what we can influence and what is outside our control makes uncertainty feel less overwhelming. And compassion is about caring, not carrying.
Tash

items.title: This Adorable, Orphaned Baby Walrus Was Rescued by Two Researchers in Alaska. Now, He's Found a New Home in Florida
items.desc: The scientists were conducting fieldwork on a remote beach in northwestern Alaska when they spotted the roughly 5-month-old calf. The little one, named Annautaq, will not be able to return to the wild because he requires constant human care and will become too habituated to people
items.text:
A baby walrus left an orphan in Alaska has found a permanent home at SeaWorld Orlando after a days-long rescue mission and extensive rehabilitation period.
On September 11, college student Violet Anniskett was conducting research on a remote beach in northwestern Alaska when she saw something completely unexpected between a pair of adult walrus carcasses: a lone calf, alive.
“I was in shock,” she tells Ishani Desai at the New York Times . As part of an internship, she had been surveying the beach with Tony Fischbach , a wildlife biologist with the U.S. Geological Survey. The duo was looking for fresh Pacific walrus carcasses that they could sample to test for algal toxins to better understand the animals’ baseline levels.
The researchers quickly requested approval from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the local Inupiaq community, which Anniskett is a member of, to rehabilitate the roughly 5-month-old male calf. They named him Annautaq (pronounced “ah-NOW-tuq”), after Anniskett’s father.
“It’s a big part of our culture that we harvest animals for subsistence living,” she tells Casey Grove at Alaska Public Media . “It was very important for us to ask the community first, and as soon as they decided as a whole, then we’re able to move forward with the steps of saving him through the SeaLife Center.”
Still, there were many steps to come. After receiving the proper permissions, the approximately 185-pound calf had to get to the Alaska SeaLife Center, the state’s only permanent marine mammal rehabilitation facility, more than 800 miles away in the southern city of Seward. Stormy weather conditions meant that they couldn’t move the hefty little walrus for days, leaving the two researchers to care for Annautaq on their own as predators loomed.
“When we found him, a determined flock of gulls was intent on scavenging him. He was in immediate peril of suffering this fate had we not gotten approval to intervene. Two polar bears were also active on the island,” Fischbach says in a statement .
The two researchers guided Annautaq to an abandoned building that could shelter him from hungry onlookers and stayed there with him for nearly four days. Walrus calves rely solely on their mother’s milk, but Anniskett and Fischbach didn’t have any formula on hand. So, they fed him a mixture of honey and water, reports the Times .
Adult male Pacific walruses can grow to up to 12 feet long and weigh up to two tons .

items.desc: More than five decades after hordes of prehistoric bones were unearthed from three caves in Granada, new forensic techniques show how communities continued to consume their dead across distinct cultural eras
items.text:
For generations, human cannibalism in prehistoric Europe was viewed as a desperate response to starvation. Now, a forensic re-examination of three prehistoric cave sites in southern Spain reveals that people ate human remains as a ritual for millennia, including after violent clashes or as a standard funeral rite.
Researchers analyzed 967 skeletal fragments representing at least 60 individuals recovered from the caves of Malalmuerzo , Carigüela and Majolicas in the province of Granada . Using high-resolution microscopy, machine learning and radiocarbon dating, the team discovered that these grisly feasts were not confined to a single crisis, such as war or starvation. Instead, they unfolded in “context-dependent episodes” between roughly 5300 B.C.E. and 3760 B.C.E., according to a recent study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science .
The bone assemblages were first excavated in the 1970s under the direction of Miguel C. Botella , a forensic anthropologist at the University of Granada. Fifty years later, Botella joined a multi-disciplinary team to subject the historical collection to modern forensic analysis.

items.title: While Cleaning Out Her Aunt's Manhattan Apartment, a Woman Found a Long-Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Buried Beneath Fur Coats in the Closet
items.desc: Painted in 1930, "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I" sat in the closet for 40 years, with only a single photograph, by O'Keeffe’s husband, Alfred Stieglitz, attesting to its existence. It could fetch upwards of $3 million at auction this month
items.text:
Most people’s closets are littered with life’s spare change—broken umbrellas, unpaired socks and discarded scraps of elementary school artwork. But while cleaning out her elderly aunt’s New York City apartment, one woman made a staggering discovery in the closet. Underneath a pile of fur coats sat a Georgia O’Keeffe landscape painting that had been tucked away for four decades.
When she made the discovery, Betsy, who asked to be referred to by only her middle name, was shocked. “I thought, ‘Wow. That’s pretty wild,’” she tells the New York Post ’s Natalie O’Neill.
The 1930 painting, Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I , is thought to be the first in a series of three paintings depicting Lobo Peak in northern New Mexico. (The second is at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the third is in a private collection.) It will hit the auction block as part of Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale on November 17. Estimates place the piece’s value between $3 million and $5 million.
“To uncover a seminal work—representative of this 20th century master’s deep personal engagement with the landscape, a pillar of her career, which is exquisitely rendered and well preserved—is a once-in-a-lifetime moment and absolutely thrilling,” Tylee Abbott, head of American Art at Christie’s New York, says in a statement .
The artwork features warm earth tones and soft, rippling hills, an early iteration of the abstracted New Mexico landscapes she would paint throughout her career.
“O’Keeffe goes to New Mexico in 1929, and this picture is from 1930, so it’s the ground floor of her inspiration at that time,” Abbott tells CBS News ’ Noelle Lilley. “And she is very vocal about, in her writings and things, about how impactful it was on her. I think you get that in this picture.”
Betsy’s aunt, a career Foreign Service worker and world-ranked bridge master, acquired Near Abiquiu in 1963. It was a graduation gift from her parents, purchased directly from O’Keeffe’s New York dealer for $3,800, roughly $42,000 today.
She displayed the modernist piece in her New York apartment for decades. But one day in the mid-1980s, in the middle of a bridge game, she noticed a guest eyeing the painting a little too closely. Out of an abundance of caution, she hid the piece in her entry closet, carefully enclosing the 10-by-24-inch painting in its original box and tucking it behind rows of fur coats.

“I think she was fully aware of its value,” Betsy explains to the Post .

items.text:
It’s a time-honoured treatment and rubbing certainly helps, but other leaves could be just as good
I f you’ve ever brushed against a stinging nettle, chances are someone told you to find a dock leaf. The wide green leaves of dock plants seem to grow conveniently nearby, and rubbing one on a sting is a time-honoured remedy. But does it actually work?
Probably not in any way that’s unique to the plant, says John Tregoning, a professor at Imperial College London and the author of Live Forever? A Curious Scientist’s Guide to Wellness, Ageing and Death .
When you brush against a nettle, tiny hairs on the plant can pierce the skin and release a mixture of chemicals, including histamine, acetylcholine and serotonin. These trigger burning, itching and redness.
Could dock leaves contain chemicals that counteract the sting, such as antihistamines? “Maybe, but probably not,” says Tregoning. There is little evidence that dock leaf sap contains substances capable of significantly relieving the reaction.
So why do people swear by them? Rubbing a leaf against the skin may provide a competing sensation that temporarily distracts from the pain, says Tregoning. “There’s a limit to the number of sensations that the nerve cells can process, so if you overstimulate them with the rubbing there’s less feedback from the pain.”
The distraction of searching for the leaves may also help. “The short burst of pain is relieved in the time spent hunting for the dock leaves.” Tregoning suggests that applying the sap may also have a cooling or soothing effect. But none of these things are unique to dock leaves.
A small study compared dock leaves with lettuce leaves as a treatment for nettle stings in nine medical students. It found no meaningful difference between the two. Tregoning suspects that any perceived benefit is most likely to be a placebo effect.

items.desc: The probe and its twin, Voyager 2, have been hurtling through space for almost 50 years, stretching humanity's reach into interstellar space. The upcoming milestone is a testament to scientific endeavor and ingenuity
items.text:
In 1977 , Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, with the aim of studying planets in the outer solar system. Almost half a century later, the twin spacecraft have long since achieved their original mission yet are still hurtling into the unknown. In fact, Voyager 1’s status as the farthest human-made object ever will soon be exemplified by an exceptional milestone: the probe is about to reach one light-day from Earth.
The spacecraft will achieve this astronomical record on November 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern time, at which point it will be 16.094 billion miles from our planet. That’s the distance light travels in 24 hours. (For context, it takes just over eight minutes , on average, for the sun’s light to reach Earth.)
“I just never imagined [the mission] would last that long,” Linda Spilker , a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), tells Science News ’ Lisa Grossman. Spilker first joined the Voyager team just before the spacecraft launched, per the outlet, and is now the Voyager project scientist.
Voyager 1 took the famous image of Earth called Pale Blue Dot in 1990. The photo inspired astronomer Carl Sagan’s book Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space, in which he wrote, “Look at that dot. That’s here. That’s home. That’s us.”
Nothing special will happen to the spacecraft when it crosses the one-light-day boundary—the milestone is purely symbolic. And yet this symbolic event marks an extraordinary feat of science, technology and space exploration made possible by the Voyager team’s continuous problem-solving. The geriatric space probes are on their last legs, and mission scientists on Earth have had to find creative ways to preserve energy, including shutting down non-essential instruments.
When the twin spacecraft launched nearly 50 years ago, they each had ten functioning instruments. Today, Voyager 1 has only two remaining : the magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields, and the plasma wave subsystem, which detects oscillations of charged particles . items.text:
Takumi Kama, “The First Appearance KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L162×W130.3×H3.5cm(F100)
In Japanese pop culture, a kaiju is a mythical monster of great proportions. They have long been symbols of chaos and destruction, serving society as cathartic vehicles to dealing with difficult times and challenging situations. In media, they could symbolically manifest as World War II and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, or natural disasters that make humankind feel powerless in the face of nature. More than anything, though, kaiju represent the consequences of human actions—or inactions.
These fantastical creatures inspired Japanese artist Takumi Kama to tackle a more recent and universal topic. In his aptly titled KAIJU series, these towering beasts aren’t made of flesh and blood. Instead, their bodies are an accumulation of the things we consume and quickly discard, whether physical or digital. “In other words,” the artist says, “it exists like a mirror reflecting us—the very people who are looking at this work—and perhaps it could even be described as a self-portrait of us as human beings.”
These kaiju loom in dark alleys and the morning fog, for which they can be accidentally run into. Some feature imagery from the Edo period, as the artist wonders how these creatures would have looked in that time, while others are more contemporary, made up of pixels or pop culture, junk food, and plastic trinkets.
Kama recently presented his work at Art Taipei, where he was one of the most talked about creatives for his unique approach to modern culture and our increasingly digitalized lives. As such, COMBINE/BAMI Gallery , which represents the artist, will offer plenty of chances to check out the artist’s work from up close. From late December 2026 through early January 2027, the gallery will present many of Kama’s works in an annual exhibition centered on the theme of the Chinese zodiac, spotlighting the artist’s charming and playful style.
Next year, COMBINE/BAMI Gallery will open a dual exhibition featuring Kama and fellow Japanese painter Hisashi Matsumoto in March. Before that, his work will be exhibited at Osaka International Art 2027, taking place January 29-31, 2027 (VIP Preview on January 28, 2027).

Up to 900 artificial nest "cups" for threatened house martins are set to be installed in Hampshire as part of a conservation project.

Between 1995 and 2024, the UK House Martin population fell by 40%, partly due to poor breeding success.

Each April and May, house martins return from Africa to spend the summer in the UK.

Modern homes tending to have uPVC soffits also makes it difficult for mud nests to adhere.
Last year the Hampshire Ornithological Society initiative launched a survey, allowing members of the public to record house martin nest locations .

An English mayor-turned-detective solved the case of a thief who was looting $9,000 worth of historic capstones from a 300-year-old stone village wall—and he used a hi-tech tracker and a little trickery.
Around 30 stones went missing over a period of months from an 18th-century wall along a half-mile stretch of road leading into Rufford, Lancashire.
Lancashire Police said they were unable to help as the area had no CCTV coverage or “forensic opportunities”.
So Councillor Matt Smith and other locals decided to take matters into their own hands.
Instead of tolerating the loss, he placed an Apple AirTag inside one of the remaining stones which was already loose, hoping it would be stolen, with the GPS tracker revealing the perpetrator’s location.
“The audacity of him to steal from the community for his own personal gain,” said the 43-year-old local official. “That isn’t what we stand for.”
Worried locals noticed the wall was first attacked and stones were taken in May, with two further raids taking place in June and October.
Matt and other residents first put up signs saying “Smile, you’re on camera”, but that didn’t deter the criminal. They also thought about installing their own CCTV cameras, but it was “too expensive” for the small hamlet.

Within weeks, he woke up to find notifications on his phone revealing the stone had been moved overnight. He then contacted the police, passing on the whereabouts.
After the stones were found in his backyard, a 41-year-old Manchester man was arrested and sentenced.
On the scene police found a substantial number of coping stones from the vandalized wall, reportedly worth around £7,000 / $9,300—but Matt claims dozens of others were also found from across the country, making the estimated total value of up to £40,000.

Out in the Pacific Ocean, halfway between California and Hawaii, lies a massive collection of human-made debris that spans an area roughly twice the size of Texas . Known as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, its accumulation of microplastics has now grown so large that it seems to be changing the color of the ocean.
Twenty years of satellite data suggests that the water in and around the trash pile has become more blue-green. Though the researchers couldn’t confirm microplastics are behind the color shift, computer simulations hint that that is likely the case. The findings, published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment on November 5, could help experts identify the most heavily polluted areas of the ocean to guide cleanup efforts.

The color of the ocean reflects whatever is in its upper layer. That’s why it’s usually blue ; water absorbs longer, redder wavelengths of light and scatters shorter, bluer wavelengths. Other elements, like sediment and microscopic organisms called phytoplankton, can affect the ocean’s hue, since sunlight interacts with those objects differently. Millions of people with high blood pressure stand to benefit from a new drug that has stunned doctors by reversing a common cause of the condition for years after patients stopped taking the medication.
Patients who took the drug, called baxdrostat, saw their blood pressure improve during a six- to 12-month course of the daily pills, but unexpectedly the benefits remained up to two years later, with some patients no longer on any hypertension drugs and potentially cured of the condition.
“It’s very exciting to see,” said Prof Morris Brown, a hypertension specialist at Queen Mary University of London, who led the study. “Just under a quarter of the patients came off all treatment and had completely normal blood pressure.”
More than a billion people worldwide have high blood pressure, or hypertension, including more than 12 million in the UK. In 5 to 10% of cases, the condition is caused by small nodules or benign tumours on the adrenal glands that cause them to overproduce a hormone called aldosterone. The excess hormone raises blood pressure by signalling the kidneys to retain salt.
The standard treatment for what is called primary aldosteronism is to surgically remove the affected adrenal gland, but other factors can contribute to the patient’s hypertension, meaning surgery is not always a complete cure.
Baxdrostat is known as an aldosterone synthase inhibitor (ASI) which suppresses the blood pressure-raising hormone. The drug was approved in the US earlier this year for patients with hypertension that is not controlled by existing drugs. It is being assessed by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice), which could make the drug available through the NHS next year.
The potentially curative effect of baxdrostat came to light in a small study that followed 14 patients whose hypertension improved dramatically during a three-month trial of the drug. They continued taking the daily pills for six to 12 months and then stopped. When doctors checked the patients up to two years later, their blood pressure was still lower. Details are published in the New England Journal of Medicine .

A ban on industrial scallop dredging has been “the most amazing thing to happen” to the residents, both man and marine, of the Summer Isles.

A painting by Wassily Kandinsky , looted during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, has sold for £31.56 million (approximately $42 million) at Christie’s London. Completed in 1907, Das bunte Leben (The Colorful Life) was returned to the descendants of its original Jewish owners in 2023. Its October 14, 2026 auction result far exceeded the presale estimate of £18 million to £25 million.
Measuring approximately 5 by 4 feet, Das bunte Leben is an important early work by the Russian-born artist. It depicts a group of figures in a colorful, imagined landscape inspired by Russian folklore. The painting also reflects Kandinsky’s growing interest in expressive color and simplified forms, which would later inform his experiments with abstraction.
Dutch Jewish collectors Emanuel and Hedwig Lewenstein acquired the painting in 1927 and later loaned it to the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam. Following the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, the work appeared at auction in October 1940 without the family’s authorization. The Lewensteins received no proceeds. It subsequently passed through several private collections before German bank Bayerische Landesbank acquired it in 1972. The painting later entered a long-term loan to Munich’s Lenbachhaus museum.
The Lewenstein descendants spent decades pursuing the painting’s restitution. In 2023, a German advisory commission on Nazi-looted art determined that Nazi persecution had forced the family to lose the work. The commission recommended its return, and the painting was subsequently restituted to the heirs, ending decades of contested ownership.
More than a century after its creation, Das bunte Leben has returned to the art market with its provenance restored. Its $42 million sale marks a new chapter for the Kandinsky painting, following its long-awaited return to the family from whom it was taken.

On November 14, 1940, German bombers obliterated the cathedral, making it the only British cathedral destroyed during the Blitz . But the earliest map-makers for Ordnance Survey, which this week marked the 225th anniversary of its first publication, might have empathised with the obsessive dedication.
The 1801 OS map of Kent was 10 years in the making, its military-led production inspired by fears of Napoleonic invasion. But as Rachel Hewitt points out in Map of a Nation , her stirring account of the Ordnance Survey’s early years, its genesis also lay in an Enlightenment-based enthusiasm for comprehending and accurately representing reality. During the course of the 19th century, the entirety of the British isles was meticulously mapped through fog, rain, wind and sun, in what was described as “a wild and arduous exercise”. The surveyors, armed with theodolites, measuring chains and notebooks, saw themselves as footsoldiers serving in the ranks of Reason as they brought intellectual order to the landscape.

Sniffer dogs are being trained in Germany to detect potentially destructive invasive plants—alien species that are one of the main causes of biodiversity loss worldwide.
Scientists from Leipzig evaluated whether volunteer handlers and their dogs could be trained as effective detectives, and found the teams could locate invasive species in the wild with 75% accuracy.
Other methods to combat invasive species have been costly and time-consuming, and the lack of effective early-detection methods has limited ecologists’ ability to control further colonization by invasive species.
Dr. Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth and her colleagues at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) tested the feasibility of a volunteer dog-handler training program, so citizen scientists could join the fight.
31 dogs and their owners were trained between 2021 and 2023 using three highly problematic invasive plant species: Himalayan balsam, common ragweed, and those in the knotweed family, such as Japanese knotweed ( Fallopia spp. complex, Impatiens glandulifera, and Ambrosia artemisiifolia ).
The training culminated with a field test of the dogs’ ability to locate target species in the wild. Of the 12 teams that completed the field test, 11 teams passed, with an average detection success rate of 75%.
From the feasibility study, published in the journal PLOS One, the research team developed a set of recommendations to improve effectiveness of future, similar projects to improve volunteer selection and coordination, dog training, and initial deployments.
“Our study shows that trained volunteer dog-handler teams have real potential to support the early detection of invasive plants,” said Dr. Grimm-Seyfarth , in a media release.
“What we find particularly exciting is the opportunity to turn something people already love doing—spending time outdoors with their dogs—into a meaningful contribution to biodiversity conservation.”
“By combining dogs’ remarkable sense of smell with the enthusiasm of citizen scientists, we could expand monitoring efforts.
“With the right training, everyday walks could become an additional resource for detecting invasive plants early.”

Doctors have made a potentially significant breakthrough in the hunt for a treatment for stiff person syndrome, the autoimmune condition that affects the singer Céline Dion .
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disease that attacks the central nervous system and can cause devastating rigidity throughout the body and painful muscle spasms. Despite decades of research, there is no cure.
Now a team of neurologists in the US trialling a novel form of immunotherapy have reported “exciting” and “very encouraging” results: the treatment has prompted dramatic improvements in people living with SPS.
Patients who previously needed help with basic daily tasks and struggled to walk have regained their ability to take part in everyday life, with some even returning to work and resuming hobbies, according to doctors at the Mayo Clinic.
The novel treatment, CAR-T cell therapy, is already used to treat cancer, and reprogrammes a patient’s immune cells to help fight disease. During the study, SPS patients’ own T cells, a type of immune cell, were extracted and engineered to wipe out disease-causing cells.
Neurologists said the results, published in medical journal Jama Neurology, were particularly exciting because patients had been able to return to activities they feared they would never be able to return to.
Dr Anastasia Zekeridou, a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, said: “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients.
“With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function. These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time.”
Jonathan Walden, one of the patients in the trial, had reached the point where walking and basic daily tasks required help from his family. But after CAR-T, he has returned to work.
“I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.”

“It was like looking for a needle in a haystack.”
That’s how Professor Daniel Mège described the discovery of trace volcanic gases on Mars that could be key to finding life on the Red Planet.
The discovery centers around hydrogen chloride gas seeping out through volcanic rifts—something of a “smoking gun” that suggests Mars is not geologically dead, but merely sleeping.
These gases hint at magma, which, when coming into contact with groundwater can produce warm habitable niches for organisms beneath the Red Planet’s surface.
“If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface,” one of the scientists behind the discovery hypothesized.
Mars is studded with the largest volcanoes in the solar system, and fresh fissures on the surface of one of the largest, called Alba Mons, hint at volcanically active spots under the surface.
Detected by a European Space Agency (ESA) orbiter, an international research team believes that the release of hydrogen chloride from these fissures comes from hot magma beneath the surface.
The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first reported hydrogen chloride gas in the Martian atmosphere in 2021. The gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, leading researchers to wonder whether the same was happening on Mars.
Evidence for active volcanism on Mars has always been extremely elusive, yet enough has been identified in the form of geologically-recent lava flows and “marsquakes” over the last 50 years, so as never to rule it out.
Now again, researchers noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride where they shouldn’t have been, and during an odd season in the northern hemisphere of Mars.
Study co-leader Professor Daniel Mège, from the Space Research Center of the Polish Academy of Sciences, said the gas varies seasonally on Mars, reaching its maximum in the northern winter, then mostly disappearing in the summer.
But there was one exception to the pattern, always in the same season and at the same place: above volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer.
A close look at the Alba Mons region using TGO’s infrared spectroscopy instrument showed fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of yards in length, associated with color changes on the surface.
